title: Cristiano Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodríguez
description: Ronaldo has five children in total, two of whom he shares with Rodríguez.She has also helped to raise his other three children, and the family current
body: Ronaldo has five children in total, two of whom he shares with Rodríguez.She has also helped to raise his other three children, and the family currently live in the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh.The couple's first daughter together, Alana Martina, was born in 2017. Their youngest daughter Bella was born in April 2022, alongside a twin brother, who died.Ronaldo has scored nearly 1,000 goals in a career which has seen him play for Lisbon-based Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus, Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia and Portugal.Ronaldo, who is currently the captain of the Portuguese football team, recently played in his sixth and final World Cup - a record for appearances in the men's finals which he shares with Lionel Messi of Argentina.The 41-year-old has won the Ballon d'Or five times, the second-highest number of wins behind Messi who has won the top footballing prize eight times.His current club Al-Nassr - which he joined in 2022 - confirmed last year that he had signed a new two-year contract, meaning he will stay with the Riyadh-based club until 2027.Last year, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index valued Ronaldo's net worth at $1.4bn (£1.04bn), making him the first billionaire football player.

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodríguez

title: Woman pulled alive from rubble 36 hours after Colombia quake
description: A 32-year-old woman, who had been trapped under rubble for 36 hours following the 7.4-magnitude quake which shook western Colombia, has been rescued a
body: A 32-year-old woman, who had been trapped under rubble for 36 hours following the 7.4-magnitude quake which shook western Colombia, has been rescued alive.Daniela Largo was pulled from beneath a collapsed building in the city of Pereira after a 10-hour-long rescue operation. Firefighters finally managed to reach her via a tunnel they dug below four concrete slabs under which she had been buried.At least 188 have died in the quake, according to official figures, and hundreds remain missing. In Pereira, a city in Colombia's coffee-growing region, 79 people are confirmed to have died, the second-highest number after Cali, where 95 are dead, according to figures by the Association of Colombian Capital Cities (Asocapitales).Largo's mother told AFP news agency that a local resident had heard her daughter cry out for help from beneath the rubble.Once emergency workers had arrived at the site, they were able to locate Largo with the help of a small camera.However, her rescue was complicated by the fact that four heavy concrete slabs were blocking the way.Local firefighters aided by colleagues deployed from the capital, Bogotá, and the disaster response team of the national police force had to dig two tunnels to reach her. Through one opening, dug from above, they were able to provide Largo with oxygen. But it was only through a second tunnel, dug from below, that they were able to free her. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella celebrated her rescue on social media, describing it as "news which fills us with hope".Largo's mother said that "at home, her 12-year-old son is waiting for her".In Pereira, at least 92 buildings collapsed. Fifteen people are known to be trapped and another 37 have been reported missing, according to Asocapitales. In Cali, Colombia's third most populous city, more than 200 people remained trapped as of 16:00 local time on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Woman pulled alive from rubble 36 hours after Colombia quake

title: Israeli settlers besieging Palestinian families in West Bank village
description: Israeli settlers have been besieging two Palestinian families in their homes in the occupied West Bank since Sunday, with the families saying their su
body: Israeli settlers have been besieging two Palestinian families in their homes in the occupied West Bank since Sunday, with the families saying their supplies were running out and rights groups urging the authorities to step in.On Wednesday Israeli security forces were reported to have withdrawn from the Jewish settler outpost in the village of Qusra near Nablus, following clashes with a crowd of extremist settlers. About a dozen settlers are said to remain at the site.After the Palestinian homeowners made their initial report to the Israeli army, the first soldiers who arrived at the scene were filmed praying with the settlers.The Abu Ridi and Hassan families have been posting on social media appealing for help after their water and power supplies were cut off and their food stocks ran low.The latest developments come as a top UN official told the Security Council in New York on Tuesday that "the West Bank is at breaking point".All settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts are set up without official Israeli authorisation.Palestinian security camera footage shows settlers tearing down a wall outside the Abu Ridi family's home on Sunday evening and using the stones to block the road.This left seven people - including two young girls – unable to leave their homes while other Palestinians could not reach them. They live in what is known as Area B, part of the West Bank under Palestinian administrative control and Israeli security control.Posting on Facebook, Qusay Abu Ridi said the situation was critical, "especially as we are completely isolated." He wrote: "We are living in our own home, on our own land, and we are asking for nothing more than the right to live safely and with dignity."On Monday, Israeli settlers blocked Israeli journalists from the left-leaning Haaretz newspaper from trying to reach the Palestinian properties. The reporters said Israeli soldiers at the scene refused to help them when their car was blocked for two hours. They were told the area was a closed military zone, however the order was not enforced on the settlers.A day later the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din urgently appealed to the head of the Israeli military's Central Command for the army to protect the besieged residents, evacuate the settlers' outpost and hold the settlers accountable.Late on Tuesday, a Palestinian ambulance was finally allowed to reach the families, delivering food and taking one child away for medical treatment.At about the same time, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) put out a statement condemning the establishment of the new outpost. It said that entering and seizing Palestinian homes was "illegal, reprehensible, and unacceptable activity".When the head of its Central Command, Maj Gen Avi Bluth and other senior officers arrived at the scene early on Wednesday they are said to have met residents and voiced their "grave concern".Afterwards, Palestinian security camera video shared with the BBC showed confrontations between Israeli soldiers and border police and a large crowd of settlers. The security forces used tear gas and stun grenades.In other footage, the Israeli forces appear to have confiscated the canopy under which the settlers were sheltering, while leaving their other equipment."Border Police forces evacuated the tent and are working to evacuate the civilians who were staying there. The incident is still ongoing," the IDF stated.It said it was decided that "disciplinary action would be taken against the security personnel involved, who were documented at the site several days ago".The Palestinian village mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, told the BBC that local residents had seen "a clear and sustained pattern of targeting Qusra". Last month a newly completed mosque was set on fire with graffiti in Hebrew sprayed nearby.That settler attack was one of many that followed on from an incident in the Palestinian village of Tal. After Israeli settlers attacked Tal, it triggered an escalation in which six people were killed - four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers – one of whom acted as a security coordinator for a nearby Israeli settlement.In July, settlers also surrounded a Palestinian home in the village of Jalud, near Qusra, for more than two weeks. Afterwards, the owners fled and settlers took over the property where they remain until now."Settler violence has reached unprecedented levels," the UN's Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, told the Security Council in a briefing on Tuesday.He gave what he described as "the sobering human toll" and mentioned that the Nablus Governorate in particular had been hit hard recently by violence.According to the UN's figures, 76 Palestinians – including 18 children - have been killed in the West Bank this year, by Israeli forces or settlers. At the same time, three Israelis – including one civilian – were killed in confrontations with Palestinians and in an alleged ramming attack by a Palestinian in the West Bank.Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities in the West Bank have experienced full or partial displacement, including 47 that have been entirely displaced, affecting more than 6,390 Palestinians, the UN says.It has registered that in 2026, about 3,800 Palestinians, nearly half of them children, have been displaced due to settler violence, demolitions and evictions.Speaking at the UN meeting, Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon dismissed the idea that settlements were an obstacle to peace. He said that they would remain and continue to grow as his country had biblical, historic and legal rights to the land.He said that the Security Council "must understand a simple truth: we are not going anywhere."

schema.headline: Israeli settlers besieging Palestinian families in West Bank village

title: How to get a good night's sleep during hot weather
description: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 25 June 2026A period of extreme heat across the UK this week has broken records for the hottest day and night temper
body: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 25 June 2026A period of extreme heat across the UK this week has broken records for the hottest day and night temperatures ever recorded in June.It can be hard to sleep during periods of hot weather, but these simple tips could help. 1. Don't let yourself napHot weather can make you feel tired and lethargic during the day. That is because you are using more energy to regulate your internal temperature.But if your sleep is disturbed at night, try to avoid napping during the day. When it is hot, feeling sleepy can be precious - save it for bedtime.2. Keep to your normal routinesHot weather can encourage you to change your habits. Don't. That can disrupt your sleep patterns. Try to keep to your usual bedtime routine, and do the things you normally do before bed.3. Remember the basicsTake steps to make sure your bedroom is as cool as it can be at night.During the day, close the curtains or blinds to keep out the sun. Make sure you shut the windows on the sunny side of your home, to keep out hot air.Open all the windows before you go to bed, to get a through breeze.4. Use thin sheetsReduce your bedding but keep covers handy. Thin cotton sheets will absorb sweat. Wearing loose-fitting clothes made of natural fibres like cotton or linen can keep you cooler than sleeping naked. However hot it is in your bedroom, your body temperature will fall during the night. That is why you sometimes wake up feeling cold even though the temperature is higher than usual. 5. Use a fan and chill your socksUsing even a small fan can be sensible in hot weather, especially when it is humid.It encourages the evaporation of sweat and makes it easier for your body to regulate your internal temperature.If you don't have a fan, try filling a hot water bottle with ice cold liquid instead.Alternatively, cool socks in the fridge and put those on. Cooling your feet lowers the overall temperature of your skin and body.6. Stay hydratedYou should make sure you drink enough water throughout the day but should avoid drinking very large amounts before bed.Image source, Getty ImagesIt's about striking the right balance. You don't want to wake up thirsty - but you don't want to have to take an additional trip to the bathroom in the early hours either.7. But think about what you drinkBe careful about soft drinks. Many contain large amounts of caffeine, which stimulates the central nervous system and makes you feel more awake.Avoid drinking too much alcohol as well. Many people drink more when the weather is hot.Alcohol might help you fall asleep but it also promotes early morning waking and a poorer quality of sleep overall.8. Stay calm - and leave your phone aloneIf you are struggling to sleep, get up and do something calming. Try reading, writing, or even folding your washing.But avoid using your phone. Mindless scrolling might seem appealing, but the blue light from the screen can stimulate your brain and leave you feeling more awake. Return to bed when you feel sleepy.9. Keep to the usual bath and bed times for childrenChildren are often quite robust sleepers - but they can be very sensitive to changes in family "mood" and routine.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lukewarm baths can help before bedtime during hot weatherMake sure usual bedtimes and bath times do not go out of the window just because it is warm.As part of the bedtime routine, the NHS UK website, external recommends lukewarm baths. Make sure they are not too cold, as that will boost your child's circulation which could increase their temperature.A baby cannot let you know if they are too hot or too cold, so it is important to monitor their temperature. They generally sleep best when their bedroom temperature is between 16C and 20C - use a room thermometer to check. 10. Remember that you will be OKMost of us need about seven to eight hours of good-quality sleep each night to function properly.Teenagers, children and babies typically need more sleep because they are still growing.But remember that the majority of people can still function well after a night or two of disturbed sleep.Although you might yawn a little more frequently than usual, you will probably be fine.These tips were based on suggestions by Prof Kevin Morgan, former director of the Clinical Sleep Research Unit at Loughborough University, and Lisa Artis, of the Sleep Council. This article was first published in July 2019.

schema.headline: How to get a good night's sleep during hot weather

title: Pep Chavarria: The late bloomer left-back joining Chelsea
description: Born in Figueres, a city in Catalonia in north-eastern Spain, Chavarria played for his hometown club before moving to Olot, where he built his reputat
body: Born in Figueres, a city in Catalonia in north-eastern Spain, Chavarria played for his hometown club before moving to Olot, where he built his reputation in Spain's lower tiers.A move to Real Zaragoza in 2020 gave him his first taste of professional football at a bigger club, and - after two seasons in Spain's second division - he earned the opportunity to step into La Liga with Rayo Vallecano in 2022.That timing was significant. Rayo were not expected to compete with Spain's established giants, but under a strong collective structure they became one of the division's most difficult opponents.Rayo's ability to compete against wealthier clubs has repeatedly relied on identifying undervalued players and maximising their strengths, and Chavarria became another example of that model - joining for less than £2m.At Vallecas, Chavarria developed into a dependable top-flight full-back, combining defensive aggression with the physicality required to succeed in the role.He made 125 appearances for Rayo and became a regular presence on the left side of defence.Joining Rayo also gave him the chance to play in front of world-class managers such as Xabi Alonso, who he faced last season when Alonso was in charge of Real Madrid.In the goalless draw with Real Madrid at Vallecas in November, Chavarria produced an excellent defensive performance - showing the aggression and discipline required to deal with elite attacking players.His performance left an impression on Alonso and Chavarria became a key target for the Spanish coach after he was appointed Chelsea manager.He also started for Rayo in last season's Conference League final, where they suffered a 1-0 defeat by Crystal Palace.Alongside new right-back Marco Palestra, who joined Chelsea for £47m from Atalanta in July, Chavarria's arrival gives Alonso the chance to replicate his wing-back system that helped Bayer Leverkusen win the Bundesliga title in 2024.His signing also adds depth to the left-back position after Marc Cucurella joined Real Madrid in June for £51.8m.Getting the deal over the line has not been easy for Chelsea, who were initially told by Rayo Vallecano that they would not sell Chavarria unless his release clause, now worth £42.4m, was met.Talks were described as "complicated" by multiple BBC Sport sources after Rayo made it clear they wanted the release clause paid in full. They believed the price was justified, with sources at the club arguing that Chavarria's underlying statistics show he plays at a similar level to Cucurella.He scored once last season and made three assists in all competitions, creating 27 chances from open play in La Liga.Furthermore, Chavarria had four years remaining on his contract and Rayo's successful player-trading model has left the club in a strong financial position, allowing them to resist offers in a similar way to Spain's traditional big three of Real Madrid, Barcelona and Atletico Madrid.That profitability also means Rayo would be liable for a 25% tax charge on any additional profit generated from a sale, reducing the net value of any fee received.

schema.headline: Pep Chavarria: The late bloomer left-back joining Chelsea

title: England training with smaller balls before WXV Global Series - John Mitchell
description: England gearing up for WXV with new smaller ballsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mitchell has been England head coach since 2023ByRugby union
body: England gearing up for WXV with new smaller ballsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mitchell has been England head coach since 2023ByRugby union commentatorEngland's women are in Nottingham for pre-season this month before the upcoming WXV Global Series. In the new competition, the Red Roses will take on Australia, Canada and New Zealand on home soil in September before further tests across the Atlantic against Canada again and the USA in October. The last time we saw the world champions in action they were winning another Six Nations' Grand Slam - so what's new? Head coach John Mitchell spills the beans.Smaller balls in campWorld Rugby's new size 4.5 balls - about 3% smaller but the same weight as a regulation size five - will be used for the WXV Global Series and are now in use in the England camp.Their introduction has not been without controversy. In May, England fly-half Zoe Harrison said it is "the worst decision someone has ever made".Mitchell said the attacking players and kickers were all given one to take home for the holidays but he believes "coaching" was key to the success of teams using it."If you want to get better at something, regardless of the size of the ball, it's all about coaching. So I think our girls have been well-coached," he said."I think it's too early for for me to say that it's going to help our offloading game or it's going to help out with the pass. I'm sure there's consequences as well. "There might be more contestable kicking, which is probably something that we want to keep away from our game because it's a point of difference between our game and the men's game."World Rugby held a trial for the smaller balls with female players on the top-tier Sevens circuit in November. Mitchell said the trial "certainly might help other teams" but he added conclusions would likely be drawn after the first three Tests at home.Mitchell belts out national anthem & becomes UK citizenDuring the summer break, Mitchell officially became a UK citizen, external - something he says he should have done "20 years earlier".Born and raised in New Zealand, the 62-year-old coached the All Blacks to the semi-finals of the 2003 Rugby World Cup but spent much of his early coaching career in England with Sale Sharks, Wasps and as England men's forwards coach. The citizenship test involves questions about British history and geography as well as singing the national anthem. Mitchell said his examiner was struggling to find the national anthem music for him so he happily helped her out, explaining: "'I've got it on my Apple Music, is it OK if I play it?' So I played it and I belted it out, and she goes, 'No-one's ever done that before'."I said, 'I've had plenty of practice'."Robinson 'taking on' Hunt roleImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Robinson won her first senior England cap in March 2025Last month, Gloucester-Hartpury wing Mia Venner and Exeter scrum-half Flo Robinson were awarded full-time England contracts for the first time, among 32 deals for the 2026-27 season.When asked about Venner and Robinson's contracts, Mitchell said scrum-half Robinson could be an important part of England's plans."Will we get Mo [Natasha Hunt] to the next World Cup? We don't know. So it's very important to make sure that we're growing our next player and Flo's definitely taking that on," he said. Both Gloucester-Hartpury's Hunt, at age 37, and Harlequins' Marlie Packer, 36, are double world champions and included on the Red Roses' latest contract round. But with Packer admitting she had considered retirement last season, Mitchell explained that for either player to move on, "somebody's got to come and get their jersey" first.Scarratt's workload growsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Scarratt left her role as assistant coach at Loughborough Lightning to join the England set-up permanentlyIn the off-season it was confirmed Emily Scarratt had joined the Red Roses set-up full-time as attack and backs coach.Having taken the role on an interim basis during the Six Nations, Mitchell said that the coaching group is "smarter" with Scarratt's inclusion. However, the new contract appears to come with more responsibility for the former world player of the year. Mitchell worked with Scarratt on the attack last season but that will start to evolve. He said: "When Em first started, I didn't want to overwhelm her with a with a whole lot of stuff so I gave her a pretty tight remit. "You just give away a little bit... She certainly has the ability to take the total attack."WXV an 'audition' for 2029 World CupThe new WXV Global Series doesn't have a table or a trophy attached to it - it is just Test matches. "There's no tournament to win so we can be very patient about how we go about things," said Mitchell. Among the six England games are three against Canada. Having beaten them in the 2025 Rugby World Cup final, it is difficult not to see the fixtures as anything other than a three-Test series and Mitchell thinks the prospect is "really cool".But with England travelling from Manchester to Exeter, to Twickenham, to Canada and the USA, the schedule is a test of its own."It's kind of like you're auditioning for Australia 2029 because geographically we're definitely going to be travelling some distance in this tournament," he said."So, I think we're trying to mirror that, understand how important our connections are and play exciting rugby."

schema.headline: England training with smaller balls before WXV Global Series - John Mitchell

title: Nicholas Hoult joins Harry Potter TV show - see the cast so far
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByIan YoungsCulture reporterNicholas Hoult, known for his roles in X-Men, Superman and Mad Max: Fury Road, has been cast in
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByIan YoungsCulture reporterNicholas Hoult, known for his roles in X-Men, Superman and Mad Max: Fury Road, has been cast in the hotly anticipated Harry Potter TV series.The English actor, 36, will play Hogwarts professor Gilderoy Lockhart - who was portrayed by Sir Kenneth Branagh in the films.The TV adaptation of JK Rowling's best-selling books will reach screens this Christmas, although Hoult will not be seen until season two.In the stories, Lockhart was a celebrity author of books such as Magical Me before joining Hogwarts as a Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher in Harry's second year.HBO announced the casting, external by quoting the title of Lockhart's autobiography and one of his famous lines: "Magical me indeed. Now, how many autographs would you like? Nicholas Hoult has been cast as Gilderoy Lockhart in season two of the new HBO original Harry Potter series."Image source, Aidan Monaghan/HBOImage caption, Dominic McLaughlin plays Harry Potter in the TV showHoult found fame alongside Hugh Grant in the big-screen adaptation of Nick Hornby's novel About A Boy in 2002, before going on to star in teen drama Skins.He played Hank McCoy, also known as Beast, in four X-Men movies, was Lex Luthor in the recent Superman film, was nominated for an Emmy for The Great, starred in Oscar-nominated film Nosferatu, and played the lead role in a biopic of author JRR Tolkien.He is the latest name to join the cast for the TV version of Harry Potter, which is expected to last for a decade.Harry Potter TV show: The main cast so farImage source, Lara Cornell/HBOImage caption, John Lithgow as Albus DumbledoreImage source, Lara Cornell/HBOImage caption, Paapa Essiedu as Severus SnapeImage source, Lara Cornell/HBOImage caption, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagallImage source, Aidan Monaghan/HBOImage caption, Daniel Rigby and Bel Powley as Vernon Dursley and Petunia DursleyImage source, Aidan Monaghan/HBOImage caption, Nick Frost as Rubeus HagridImage source, Aidan Monaghan/HBOImage caption, Warwick Davis as Professor Filius FlitwickImage source, David Jon/HBO MaxImage caption, And as in the films, young newcomers make up the central trio - Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter and Alastair Stout as Ron WeasleyThe show's first season - named Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone after the UK title of Rowling's first book - will be launched on HBO Max on 25 December.The author's seven books were published between 1997 and 2007, and were turned into eight films from 2001 to 2011.Rowling has since also become known for her outspoken views on the issue of gender identity. She says she is defending women's rights and has denied accusations of transphobia.Many of the TV show's adult cast members have fielded questions, external in recent years about whether they support her stance, and taken varying positions.The subject was in the headlines again this week when Bel Powley, who plays Petunia Dursley, told the Telegraph, external she "strongly disagrees" with the author.

schema.headline: Nicholas Hoult joins Harry Potter TV show - see the cast so far

title: Woman assaulted by double murderer Simon Levy says nightmare became 'real life' when police let him attack again
description: A woman who was attacked by double murderer Simon Levy eight years ago has told the BBC the police made her nightmare "real life" by letting him go on
body: A woman who was attacked by double murderer Simon Levy eight years ago has told the BBC the police made her nightmare "real life" by letting him go on to kill and attack more women.Laura, whose surname we are not using, said she had been trying to protect other women by reporting Levy in 2018, but feels betrayed by what he was later allowed to do after being released from jail.Levy was convicted on Friday of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins and raping another woman in London in 2025. He will be sentenced on Wednesday.He was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the Tube in London between 2023 and 2025.Police, prosecutors and the courts made a series of disastrous decisions that left Levy free. He attacked 14 more women before being taken off the streets, despite being a sex offender who was monitored by the Met Police.Levy was a registered sex offender because he sexually assaulted Laura – and a separate victim - in summer 2018.Laura says that Levy is "evil" and that his attack "completely changed my life".But she now realises that what she would "think about, dream about, have nightmares about was actually happening - he was actually still out preying on vulnerable women".Waiving her anonymity, she said she had been trying to protect other women by ensuring that Levy was jailed."I feel like when I reported it, I was doing the right thing and I thought I was doing it to protect other women."I feel absolutely devastated for all of those women that have been affected by him – and the families."Laura says she feels let down by the whole criminal justice system including the Met Police, the courts and judges who bailed Levy, as well as the Crown Prosecution Service."They're all as guilty for allowing him to continue to do what he was doing", she says."They could have prevented so many women from being hurt. "They could have prevented two women from losing their lives."Laura encountered Levy while with a friend travelling to the Notting Hill Carnival on the London Underground in August 2018. He latched onto them and followed them to the carnival. He then subjected her to a serious sexual assault.Laura says she forced Levy off and became "hysterical" and started "crying". With her friend, they tried to escape Levy but he kept following them. Eventually, a group of men chased him off after she told people what had happened.But when she tried to report the crime to police officers, she was turned away.She says two Met officers told her that they "were busy with other, more urgent, things".A third, female officer eventually took her details, but Laura says the officer didn't make sure she was safe, or look for Levy that day, despite Laura and her friend having a photo of him."There was a lot more things they could have done to make me feel supported", she says.Challenged on the response to Laura at the carnival, the Met Police said: "We are sorry the victim felt unsupported in this case and don't underestimate the impact this incident had on her. "A crime report was created the following day with a wide range of enquiries carried out. Levy was identified, arrested and later convicted."After later being contacted by officers, Laura gave a statement 15 days after the attack, and attended an ID parade the next year. It took three years for Levy to go to court. In 2021 he was convicted of sexually assaulting her, as well as another woman he had assaulted a month before Laura.He was jailed for three years, but released on licence despite sexually assaulting a prison officer.Laura found out Simon Levy was going to be on trial for two murders when she Googled his name earlier this year."My heart dropped in my stomach when I read that", she says.Laura says she was also shocked to discover that Levy had already been investigated for allegedly sexually assaulting another woman in 2017. He was not charged at the time, something now viewed as a mistake by the CPS and the Met."Had they charged him in 2017, I may not have even ever had to go to court. I may never have been assaulted, ever".She says there should be a societal change in the approach to male violence against women and girls."They need to look at everything, all of it, because they could have prevented so many women from being hurt. "They could have prevented two women from losing their lives."She adds: "I hope that other victims in the future will be believed, will be dealt with differently, will be listened to straightaway, and I just hope that there's change".BBC Action Line: If you have been affected by issues in this story, find out what support is available here.Do you have information about this story? Contact us on email daniel.desimone@bbc.co.uk or via the Signal messaging app @investigation.56

schema.headline: Woman assaulted by double murderer Simon Levy says nightmare became 'real life' when police let him attack again

title: European Athletics Championships: Keely Hodgkinson - why is 800m world record so tough to break?
description: The women's 800m world record is held by Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds in 1983.There have been claim
body: The women's 800m world record is held by Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds in 1983.There have been claims that Kratochvilova's performance in Munich was assisted by the systematic doping regime that existed in her country at the time - something she has strenuously denied.Kratochvilova's record is not the only one to be questioned.Marita Koch of East Germany set the women's 400m record two years later, in 1985 - when the country was known to be systematically doping its athletes.But Koch never failed a drugs test, and always maintained she did nothing wrong.In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005.The proposals never went any further. But they sent a strong signal that some records set before 2005 - when World Athletics (formerly IAAF) started storing blood and urine samples - could be disputed.Back in 1983, then 32-year-old Kratochvilova crossed the finish line more than seven seconds ahead of her closest rival, Poland's Jolanta Januchta.No-one would come within a second of Kratochvilova's record for 25 years.The closest any athlete has come to breaking it is Swiss athlete Audrey Werro, who ran a time of 1:53.80 in June this year."Believe you me, that time of 1:53.28 is astonishing," Jenny Meadows, former British runner and coach to Hodgkinson, told BBC Sport."I won medals on a global level and I could not even comprehend that a female could run that sort of time."But athletes have never been closer to breaking it.Werro has twice gone under 1:54 this year, but still more than half a second from Kratochvilova's record.Olympic champion Hodgkinson broke the 800m indoor record in February, which had stood since 2002, crossing the line in 1:54.87.Then there's the Netherlands' Femke Broeders-Bol, still largely an unknown in the 800m after deciding to switch disciplines from 400m hurdles. But, with little 800m experience, she ran a time of 1:55.60 seconds at the Paris Diamond League event in June."They're all dragging each other to these incredible times. The level of the 800m has risen significantly in the past two years," said Jessica Ennis-Hill, who won heptathlon gold at the London 2012 Olympics.Innovations in sports science have edged athletes closer too."Everyone is going faster than they used to be because the shoe technology is so much better," University of Exeter professor Andrew Jones told BBC Sport.Jones specialises in applied physiology, working with middle and long-distance runners to chase faster times."We know more about various supplements, things like creatine, nitrate, but in particular bicarbonate."And we know more about what limits performance".This includes our understanding of carbohydrates, and how to best fuel for a middle-distance race like the 800m."It's a bit like a Formula One race car," he added. "You want the car to cross the line almost empty of fuel. If you've got half a tank left, you've been weighing yourself down."Now, in Birmingham, the best three 800m runners in the world are looking like they will contest a gripping final, if they come through Thursday's semi-finals. Whether that final will turn into a more tactical race or develop into a battle of speed remains to be seen."All it takes is one person to raise the bar and you think more things are possible," Hodgkinson told BBC Sport."Everyone knows that to keep up you have to keep getting better. It's a really exciting time for the women's 800m."This article is the latest from BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team.

title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak: When and where to catch a glimpse
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, This year's Perseid peak coincides with a new moon, so there will be no bright moonlight to obscure meteorsBy
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, This year's Perseid peak coincides with a new moon, so there will be no bright moonlight to obscure meteorsByMaddie MolloyClimate & Science reporter and Matt TaylorLead Weather PresenterThe best annual meteor shower has once again returned to our skies, and the Perseids dazzling display is set to peak on Wednesday night.But skywatchers will be treated to not one, but two, impressive astronomical events within just a few hours of each other.A deep partial solar eclipse will be also visible in the UK in the early evening before the Sun sets and the stars emerge. While the two events are unrelated, their timing makes for an exceptional night of stargazing.Astronomer Dr Becky Smethurst said it was "the perfect cosmic coincidence of events".Here is when to look up and where you will have the best views of the meteor shower.What is the Perseid meteor shower?Meteor showers happen when the Earth passes through trails of debris from asteroids or comets - a snowball of frozen rock and gas orbiting the Sun. As that debris enters our planet's atmosphere, it burns up and creates spectacular streaks of light - meteors.Royal Astronomical Society Research Fellow Dr Becky Smethurst described the Perseids as "one of the best nights for astronomy all year".The Perseids, pronounced 'Per-see-ids', are caused by debris left behind specifically by the Swift-Tuttle comet.This comet is considered large with its solid core measuring 16 miles (26km) across.As it takes 133 years to complete a single orbit around the Sun - much longer than our own - some of the pieces of rock we see burning up could have been left behind more than a century ago."It's sort of like the Universe's own cosmic clock in a way," Smethurst said.These meteors are visible all around the world and named because they appear to originate from the constellation Perseus.When and where can I see it?The Perseids is active from mid-July to 23 Aug this year, but on most nights the shower will only display a few meteors each hour.But the best time to watch is on the peak nights, which this year is in the early morning hours between midnight and dawn on 12 and 13 August.At this time there will be many, many more meteors. If you are really lucky, you could see more than 100 'shooting stars' per hour.If possible, choose somewhere away from cities and artificial light. Light pollution will hide the fainter meteors, leaving only the brightest ones visible.This year could offer especially good viewing conditions because there is a new moon, meaning there will be no bright moonlight.Give your eyes around 20 to 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness and look towards the widest unobstructed area of sky possible.What is the night-sky forecast for Wednesday?For most of England and Wales, stargazers will have largely clear skies throughout the night with just a small chance of one or two mist patches.If you plan to stay up late in the very far north of England, Northern Ireland or much of Scotland you may need to employ a little more patience. While some cloud breaks are expected, there will be large areas of cloud at times and even the risk of one or two showers. For those in north-west Scotland, an early night might be a better option. The forecast may yet change so keep checking with BBC Weather for the latest details.Could I see a meteor during the eclipse?During an eclipse, the sky darkens offering a short window to also see the Perseids at the same time. But this will only be in the areas witnessing a total eclipse - like Spain - and not in the UK where only a partial eclipse will be witnessed. But even there, the chances are extremely slim, "you would have to get very, very lucky to see a shooting star during the total eclipse," Dr Smethurst said. Remember for a solar eclipse you must use certified solar glasses - looking directly at the sun without proper eye protection can cause permanent eye damage.Get in touchAre you planning to watch the Perseid meteor shower peak, and how are you preparing?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
description: Image source, The Boston Globe/Getty ImagesImage caption, Two girls look through their pinhole boxes during the partial solar eclipse in Boston, USA,
body: Image source, The Boston Globe/Getty ImagesImage caption, Two girls look through their pinhole boxes during the partial solar eclipse in Boston, USA, in 2017ByGeorge SandemanWith most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses. And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead. They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.Here are some viewing methods to try instead.Pinhole projector - card, paper and penThe astronomy group suggests creating a pinhole projector, which can be done by making a hole in a piece of card. You can use the tip of a ballpoint pen to push through the centre of it.Holding the card in one hand and a blank piece of paper in the other, face away from the Sun.Then line the card and paper up so that an image of the Sun becomes visible on the paper.This pinhole projector will show you the shadow being cast on the Sun replicated in miniature.Colander - find one in the kitchenInstead of straining vegetables and pasta, you can use a colander to achieve a similar effect to that of the pinhole projector.Eye specialist David Jones, consultant ophthalmologist at the Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust, says this is his favourite way of witnessing an eclipse."If you hold the colander to the Sun and you look away from the Sun, protecting your eyes, you can make not just one picture of the Sun but a hundred all at once."Demonstrating the technique in a video on social media, he clutches a blank piece of paper behind the colander he is holding up.It creates a kaleidoscope of images showing the Sun and the shadow cast on it during the eclipse.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A colander can be used to view the eclipse Pinhole viewer - cardboard box, foil, paperAn empty cereal box is ideal for making a pinhole viewer. It works similarly to the projector but should provide a clearer image.This is because the cardboard box blocks out the surrounding sunshine and allows in only light from the direction of the eclipse.Cut out a piece of paper that fits the bottom of the box. Open the top of the box and tape the cutout to the bottom. This will be the screen on which you see the eclipse.Close the box and tape it shut. On one half of the top of it, cut out a small square so you can see the paper at the bottom with one eye.On the other half, cut out another small square to match. Cut out a piece of foil that is large enough to cover this square.Tape it down over the square and use a pin or needle to poke a hole in the middle of the foil.Standing with your back to the Sun, use one eye to look through the open square.Once you've lined up the hole in the foil with the Sun, you should see an image of it on the screen at the bottom. This is where you'll see the eclipse too.Can I not use my phone?You might be tempted to watch or film the eclipse using your mobile phone, either by pointing it at the Sun or taking a selfie video, but Nasa advises against this., external"To take images when the Sun is partially eclipsed, you'll need to use a special solar filter to protect your camera, just as you'll need a pair of solar viewing glasses (also called eclipse glasses) to protect your eyes."They also say sensors in your phone could be damaged if pointed directly at the Sun. "This is especially true if you're using any sort of magnifying lens attachment on the phone."When the partial eclipse becomes visible in the UK and mainland Europe on Wednesday, it will be in the evening so it will take place low in the sky.For a better view, the Royal Astronomical Society advises you try standing somewhere more elevated than the area around you "with a clear view of the western horizon".Whatever you do, don't look directly at the Sun.Get in touchAre you planning to watch the Perseid meteor shower peak, and how are you preparing?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. title: Sun-tanned cauliflowers and knobbly spuds - the heatwave veg that's good to eat
description: Image source, OddboxByAlex DanielBusiness reporterWould you buy a cauliflower that looks like it's been sunburnt or a cucumber that's curled back on i
body: Image source, OddboxByAlex DanielBusiness reporterWould you buy a cauliflower that looks like it's been sunburnt or a cucumber that's curled back on itself?Farmers across the UK are grappling with one of the driest, hottest growing seasons in decades. Repeated heatwaves after a warmer than usual spring have led to predictions of the worst harvest since records began.The heat is not only affecting how much produce is grown, but also how it looks.Retailers usually reject fruit and vegetables that don't meet strict guidelines on size, shape and colour. But with supplies under pressure, many are now expected to loosen those rules rather than risk empty shelves.That means shoppers could start seeing smaller, wonkier or oddly coloured veg on the shelves in the coming weeks - and sellers and growers say it's still good to eat.'Sun-tanned' cauliflowersImage source, OddboxImage caption, This year's extreme heat is turning cauliflower heads yellow rather than whiteCauliflower is one of the most affected vegetables in hot weather because it needs lots of water.Its heads are usually shielded from sunlight by the leaves, but in this year more light is reaching them and turning them yellow.Emilie Vanpoperinghe, co-founder of Oddbox, a subscription company that sells surplus produce that supermarkets reject, said it is "purely a cosmetic defect" and the plants taste exactly the same. She said Oddbox acquired 6,000 cauliflower heads last week that were too dark for supermarkets to sell.Growers are reporting that their water reserves are depleted, Vanpoperinghe said, which means the cauliflower and broccoli family of brassicas will experience slower growth, leading to shorter supplies.That short supply means retailers may soon start stocking "sun-tanned" cauliflower because "their biggest nightmare is empty shelves", she said. "They want to make sure that they've got availability of produce all the time."Curly cucumbersImage source, Tony Charrin / OddboxImage caption, Extreme heat is also causing cucumbers to curl back in on themselvesGrowers are also reporting cucumbers that are coming out misshapen, with some bending back into a spiral.That is because the plants are grown in greenhouses which overheat in the high outdoor temperatures, causing the plants to become stressed, Vanpoperinghe said."Even if they get the irrigation then it's just extreme heat, which means the plant is not able to grow anymore."Holey pak choiImage source, John HarperImage caption, Pests that do well in the heat are eating holes in the leaves of John Harper's pak choiJohn Harper, a farmer in Worcestershire, grows pak choi for Sainsbury's, Aldi and Co-op, and has discarded more produce than usual this year because of tiny holes made by pests.Flea beetles thrive in hot, dry conditions, and farmers are no longer allowed to use as many pesticides as before, meaning net covers are Harper's only defence.Supermarkets' strict cosmetic rules mean "one tiny little hole can render the plant useless", he said, but some have temporarily loosened the rules."We've been working with them through this hot period and in general they sort of get it," he added. Harper said the vast majority of affected pak choi is still edible - even if "it seems to be quite tasty" for the beetles too.Knobbly potatoesImage source, Lucy MunnsImage caption, Hot weather can cause potatoes to grow into several separate sectionsLucy Munns, a potato farmer in Cambridgeshire, said the hot weather will stunt the root vegetable's growth, leading to oddly shaped tubers that supermarkets and chip shops, which she supplies, wouldn't normally buy.When the weather gets cooler after a hot period, instead of the main potato tuber growing "it tends to grow a little knobble on the end"."Trying to find people that will accept potatoes like that is very difficult. So that ultimately means a lot of wastage for us," Munns added. "It's criminal, to be honest, to be chucking that much food away."Those "knobbly and misshapen potatoes" however are absolutely fine to eat, she said."The only difficulty is peeling them, but just cut the knobbly bit off and peel it separately."'A challenging period'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Many supermarkets have started their own 'imperfect veg' lines in recent yearsSupermarkets including Sainsbury's, Tesco, Morrisons and Waitrose already have dedicated lines for wonky vegetables.Calum Kelly, Waitrose's produce technical manager, said in demanding weather conditions "we relax size and shape guidelines for key veg to avoid waste and provide more income to our growers and farmers"."Baking potatoes might be a little smaller than usual this harvest if the drought continues. All these veg still taste great, but like many of us in a heatwave, they might just look a little less than perfect."Not every gap can be filled this way though. Andrew Opie, the director of food and sustainability at the British Retail Consortium, said supermarkets are also importing more food from abroad as UK supplies run short."Retailers face the dilemma of supporting British farmers, but also making sure that we, as customers, have what we expect to buy when we go in the shop," he said."It's going to be a challenging period right through into the autumn. We're hearing potentially it could affect things like cherries as well."Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Supermarkets are being forced to import more produce from abroad because of the heatBritish summers are getting hotter and drier as the climate changes and heatwaves like this one are becoming more frequent. That means a season like this one may become less of a one-off, and more of a preview of what British farming has to deal with regularly.Many farmers will either have to accept more waste, invest in better irrigation and water storage systems, or find a way to sell more wonky produce to consumers.Munns, the potato farmer, said more people should try buying imperfect veg if they see it in the supermarket aisle this year.People should "be a bit less picky" about fresh produce, she said. "We've been too spoilt in the UK … In other less fortunate countries we wouldn't have a choice."Get in touchAre you involved in the agriculture industry, or do you have a related story to share?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. title: Phones banned in Edinburgh schools - but still no pouches to keep them in
description: Image source, City of Edinburgh CouncilImage caption, Mobile phones will have to be kept in magnetically sealed pouches during the school dayA mobile
body: Image source, City of Edinburgh CouncilImage caption, Mobile phones will have to be kept in magnetically sealed pouches during the school dayA mobile phone ban in Edinburgh schools has come into force - despite pouches to secure the devices not being available yet. Primary school pupils who have returned after the summer holidays will have to keep their phones in cabinets during the day, while secondary school pupils were previously told they would have to lock them in a magnetically-sealed pouch.However, the council has now said the pouches will not be ready until next month at the earliest, as the new system is still being tested. It said the ban was still in place and phones should be kept turned off and out of sight during the school day - including breaks - unless a pupil is exempt. The council said guidance on exemptions and reasonable adjustments was still being finalised.Edinburgh is one of the first councils in Scotland to bring in such widespread restrictions following trials in Portobello and Queensferry.The new policy also covers smartwatches in both primary and secondary schools.City of Edinburgh Council's education spokesman James Dalgleish said the pouches would be introduced in phases at secondary schools throughout September and October.Parents and guardians will be kept updated on when they can expect to receive pouches for their children.Dalgleish said: "We have been working very hard over the school summer holidays to navigate through the procurement process and make sure we get good value for Edinburgh taxpayers when purchasing pouches. "In a matter of weeks we will see pouches being phased into schools, with every secondary school having a pouch system in place by the start of the October break at the latest."It is about getting the final part of this complex process right, which will take a few weeks but I'm confident we'll see the benefit of the new restrictions."Image caption, Phone use is now restricted in schools in EdinburghCouncil funding of £400,000 was agreed in February to support restrictions on mobile phones and other devices in Edinburgh.Lockable pouches were trialled at Portobello and Queensferry high schools over the last school year, and a council report said it had been "broadly successful".Earlier this year, Education Secretary Màiri McAllan announced that all school learning environments would become phone-free.She urged schools across Scotland to act before the government introduced new legislation.The Scottish government introduced guidance allowing head teachers to bring in their own phone bans in schools in 2024.It came after a 2022 study, external which showed that about a third of pupils in Scottish classrooms admitted they had been distracted by the devices.Get in touchWhat stories would you like BBC News to cover from Edinburgh, Fife and the east of Scotland?

title: How affordable are Edinburgh's festivals?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByAimee Stanton and Andrew PickenBBC ScotlandUpdated 7 hours agoEdinburgh is home to one of the world's biggest cultural eve
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByAimee Stanton and Andrew PickenBBC ScotlandUpdated 7 hours agoEdinburgh is home to one of the world's biggest cultural events every summer as it is transformed into a festival city.The Scottish capital hosts the Fringe, the International Festival and the Military Tattoo alongside film, art and book festivals during August.Complaints about soaring prices in the city are nothing new – but recent years have seen increasing concerns about the cost of attending its summer festivals.So how affordable is the city for acts and audiences? BBC Scotland has analysed some of the main costs for festival-goers to see if they really are paying more.Feeling the impact of rising costsImage caption, Kaitlyn Smith says a day out at the festivals has become more expensiveKaitlyn Smith has attended the Fringe every year since moving to Edinburgh from Orkney 10 years ago.She has worked handing out flyers as a way to offset the expense of seeing a range of performances over the course of a day.The 25-year-old said the cost was the "biggest barrier" to local people getting the full festival experience."A full day out at the Fringe, you can spend £100 or £200 in a day," she said."If you are coming on holiday, you know you are coming to the Fringe. You know that you are saving up money to see it, but we're here the whole month and obviously we would like to try and do the Fringe as well."But you are paying £7 or £8 for a pint, £10 or £12 for food - that's one meal. And that's not even starting on your tickets for shows."She added: "I think the shows are worth it, but if you want to see a big volume, you just can't."What makes the city so expensive?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Royal Mile is one of the city's popular destinations during the festivalsDarren Neale, venue director at Greenside Venue in Edinburgh, told BBC Scotland that almost every cost associated with running a Fringe venue had increased significantly over the years.He said utilities, insurance, technical equipment, transport and other operational costs had risen for the venue - but housing had seen the most dramatic change."The cost of staying in Edinburgh during August has risen exponentially over the last decade, creating challenges not only for performers but also for the staff and freelancers who make the festival possible," he said."We have seen our accommodation cost rise on average by 300% in the last decade."He added: "The festival's affordability is one of the reasons it has become the world's largest arts festival, and there is a real balance to be struck between paying people fairly, covering rising costs and keeping live theatre within reach of audiences."How much have accommodation costs increased?The price of finding somewhere to stay during August has long been an issue for the city and its festivals.A slump in Fringe sales in 2022 was blamed on rising accommodation costs but sales recovered in the subsequent years, topping 2.6 million last year.Earlier this year the city lost the TV festival to Manchester, with organisers citing challenges around "accessibility, affordability and sustainability".Figures shared with BBC Scotland from commercial real estate data group Costar suggest average hotel prices have been growing year on year since 2019.The average daily room rate in 2025 was just over £260, an increase of 9% on the previous August and 64% on pre-Covid levels. In comparison, the rate was £110 in Glasgow and £81 in Manchester.Staying in self-catering accommodation is not much cheaper.Figures from Visit Britain suggest renting an entire property in Edinburgh to sleep one or two people cost visitors £204.68 a day in August in 2025. The Glasgow rate was £161.67 and it was £106.92 in Manchester.However, the price for a short-term let can vary dramatically depending on the type – such as a private or shared room within property or booking an entire home - and the number of people.Visitors staying in Edinburgh this year will also have to pay the city's new tourist tax - an additional 5% on top of their original booking cost for the first five nights.Due to a lack of publicly available data, we were unable to analyse festival accommodation costs at university-run establishments.Last year 1.5 million tickets were bought by people with an Edinburgh postcode, up from 1.4 million in 2024.But high housing costs for those living in the city are not restricted to August. Data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), external suggests the capital boasts some of the highest average rents in the country.What about the price of tickets?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Gilded Balloon at Teviot is one of the biggest Fringe venuesBut what about the cost of going to shows?We analysed the average price of the cheapest ticket at the six August festivals - nearly 600,000 shows since between 2016 and 2026 - to explore if prices have changed over the last decade.Our analysis found average ticket prices (excluding booking fees) increased in cash terms from £10 to £12.80.When adjusted for inflation, the price of this year's cheapest ticket has actually fallen over the last decade. The figure is £1.37 less than it was 10 years ago, when the average cost was £14.17.Sticking with real terms, average prices of the cheapest ticket were slightly higher before the pandemic but have broadly stayed around £12.75 since 2021 - despite the rising overheads for performers, production companies and venues.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ticket prices make for an interesting picture in EdinburghThe figures also vary by festival.Over the last decade the average lowest ticket price increased in real terms from £19.83 to £20 at Edinburgh International Festival.However, there has been a real term decrease at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, from £14.17 to £12.80.Real term prices have fallen from £17 to £15.50 at the Edinburgh International Book Festival and from £14.17 to £12 at the Edinburgh International Film Festival.Due to the nature of the event, tickets for the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo are generally more expensive than other shows.Our analysis found it saw the largest increase, with average lowest ticket prices rising by 36% from £35.41 to £48.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tickets for the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo have risen over the last decadeLori Anderson is the director of Festivals Edinburgh, an umbrella organisation for the major city festivals.She said that they are still seen as "incredible value for money" by residents and visitors alike."Costs across Edinburgh in August have risen significantly, particularly accommodation, and our festivals are actively grappling with those issues - albeit with no direct control over them," she explained."What we do control, however, are the events that happen every year."Our festivals work tirelessly to ensure tickets remain affordable for as many people as possible, putting in place ticket offers and concession prices for those who might otherwise feel excluded."Festivals Edinburgh has estimated that the events contribute £852m to Scotland's economy, external every yearAnderson added: "We cannot be complacent - our festivals want to work with partners across the city to ensure that Edinburgh is a city where everyone can afford to live, visit and perform."About the ticket sales dataUsing official listings data from Festivals Edinburgh we analysed the median lowest publicly advertised full price ticket from 2016 to 2026. Prices were adjusted for inflation using Office for National Statistics, external data to allow for comparisons over time. In the absence of ticket sales data, this allowed us to consistently measure like-for-like prices for each event, while reducing the impact of different pricing structures and models across the festivals.The analysis does not account for tickets that may have been sold at a lower price due to promotions, nor concession tickets. Pay-what-you-can, free shows and cancelled events were excluded from the analysis, as were booking fees. The analysis only includes shows that took place in June, July or August.Additional reporting from Isobel Cottam and James Delaney.

title: Homes near pylons to get £250 a year off energy bills – first sites revealed
description: The first locations where households living close to new upgraded electricity pylons and substations will receive a £250 annual discount on their bill
body: The first locations where households living close to new upgraded electricity pylons and substations will receive a £250 annual discount on their bills have been revealed.Customers living within 1,600ft (500m) of 43 transmission projects across Britain will be eligible for the payments for up to 10 years under the bill discount scheme, sometimes dubbed "pounds for pylons".UK ministers say replacing and upgrading decades-old infrastructure is vital for distributing renewable power and improving energy security.Critics, however, argue the discounts are meagre compensation for the impact on their homes, neighbourhoods, and the environment.About two-thirds of the projects are in Scotland, to support the fast-growing wind energy sector.But major upgrades are also planned across Britain, including areas north of London, as well as East Anglia, the Midlands, and North Wales. UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast the UK's power infrastructure had undergone decades of "woeful underinvestment".He said he understood the objections of those living nearby, but added the pylons were "crucial" to ensure the National Grid maintained future resilience."I totally accept that people might not like that, but it is critical national infrastructure and it has to be built somewhere," he said."Building any kind of infrastructure in these communities does cause disruption. But that doesn't mean we shouldn't build any kind of infrastructure and I'm afraid in this country, for too long, we have taken that view, and the result is that we have been held back by not having the infrastructure the country needs."Shanks added: "Either we go through decades of not upgrading the grid and take the risk that the grid will actually fail, but we also lose the opportunity of cheaper bills, homegrown power connecting."We're not prepared to take that risk."The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero says Britain's electricity grid was largely designed for an era when power came from coal and gas-fired power stations, and now needs major upgrades to cope with growing amounts of renewable energy.Ministers say the lack of capacity means some wind farms are sometimes paid to switch off because there is not enough network infrastructure available to carry the electricity to homes and businesses that need it.Greg Jackson, chief executive of the UK's biggest domestic energy supplier, Octopus Energy, said the electricity system is inefficient, brittle and expensive. He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the discount scheme was a "positive first step", adding that last year the UK spent more than £1bn paying wind farms to turn off on windy days."We should just be giving that electricity more cheaply to the people and businesses who live in the areas where we're generating it," he said."By doing that, you'd be able to stop wasting that money and instead put the electricity to use cutting bills for those people. But crucially cutting bills for everybody else as well because it's less wasteful."Approximately 80p a year will be added to all energy bills to fund the discount scheme.Most households that qualify will receive the discount automatically on their electricity bill every six months although some, such as those on commercial meters, may need to apply.The first payments will start early next year, when eligible customers will receive more information from their supplier or the energy regulator Ofgem. An assessment earlier this year estimated that between 120,000 and 160,000  households could eventually receive the discounts as more projects are rolled out. Rural campaign groups argue it is impossible to put a price on the loss of landscapes, and some residents living close to proposed projects say the money being offered is an insult. Kate Matthews of the Save Our Mearns campaign group, fighting plans for upgraded pylons in north-east Scotland including the Kintore to Tealing project, said the discount scheme was an insult. She said: "£2,500 off electricity bills over 10 years is a slap in the face for residents facing ruined businesses and unsellable homes. "This government is either massively out of touch or is showing their contempt for affected residents and energy consumers."Matthews said the plans had already caused "mental anguish" for residents who now faced a decade of development that would lead to noise, road closures, and heavy traffic."Then a lifetime of pylons impacting on their environment, agriculture, tourism, property values, physical and visual amenity to name a few," she added. The size of the pylons will vary depending on location and purpose, but in north east Scotland some the proposed latticed structures are about 187ft (57m) tall.  They would be similar in appearance to the already upgraded line running from Beauly to Denny where the pylons range from 138ft (42m) to 213ft (65m).  Many of projects involve a mix of underground and pylon supported cables, as well as sub-stations, converter stations, and equipment used in electricity transmission. Campaigners have called for greater sections of the network to be "undergrounded".But National Grid and transmission companies argue this would be significantly more expensive and make it harder to carry out repairs.

schema.headline: Homes near pylons to get £250 a year off energy bills – first sites revealed
